Since set elements may coincide, do not cancel \(a\). From \(A=B\), we need \(1,b\in B\).

- If \(a=1\), then \(A=B=\{1,b\}\) for any \(b\), so \(a+b=1+b\) is arbitrary.
- If \(a=-1\), then \(B=\{1,-1,-b\}\), and equality gives \(b\in\{-1,0,1\}\), so \(a+b\in\{-2,-1,0\}\).
- If \(ab=1\), then \(b=1/a\), and equality forces \(a=\pm1\), already covered.

Thus \(a+b\) is not uniquely determined. For example, \(a=1,b=2\) gives \(a+b=3\), while \(a=-1,b=0\) gives \(a+b=-1\).

\boxed{\text{not uniquely determined}}
